questions.q: Define "discourse linkers" and "signallers" in the context of a structured conversation like an interview, and give one example of each from the Umberto Eco interview in the textbook.
questions.a: Discourse linkers are cohesive devices (reference pronouns like "that," "this," "which" or lexical repetition) that connect utterances between speakers; signallers are explicit phrases marking topic shifts (e.g., "Which brings me to my next question," "But let me tell you another story"). From the text: linker — "Over 40" (Eco repeating Mukund's "more than 20"); signaller — "Which brings me to my next question" (Mukund shifting to The Name of the Rose). A wrong answer that confuses linkers with signallers reveals the student hasn't grasped that linkers maintain cohesion within a topic while signallers manage transitions between topics — a distinction critical for both board exam discourse analysis questions and real-time group discussion management.

questions.q: Explain in your own words why Umberto Eco says he "works in empty spaces" (interstices), and connect this to the broader theme of time management in creative work.
questions.a: Eco uses "interstices" — waiting for an elevator, gaps between appointments — as micro-slots for writing (e.g., drafting an article during an elevator ride). This reflects his philosophy that creativity doesn't require large uninterrupted blocks but thrives in fragmented time, a practical insight for students juggling board exams and competitive prep. A wrong answer that treats "interstices" as merely metaphorical without the concrete time-management application shows the student misses the chapter's pragmatic layer: the interview genre reveals not just personality but actionable life strategies, which is exactly what board "Talking about the text" discussions expect students to extract.

questions.q: In a group discussion on "Every famous person has a right to privacy; interviewers sometimes embarrass celebrities with personal questions," use the PEEL structure (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) to contribute a 90-second turn that references both Part I (Kipling/Naipaul) and Part II (Eco's comfort level).
questions.a: Point: Celebrities have a conditional right to privacy that varies by individual consent. Evidence: Part I shows Kipling calling interviews "immoral" and "cowardly," while Naipaul feels "wounded"; Part II shows Eco comfortably discussing his work habits and philosophy. Explanation: The contrast proves privacy invasion isn't inherent to the genre — it depends on interviewer ethics and interviewee boundaries. Link: Therefore, the solution isn't banning interviews but establishing ethical protocols, as Eco's willingness demonstrates. A wrong answer that only cites one part or offers opinion without textual evidence reveals the student cannot synthesize across the chapter's two sections — a skill explicitly tested in CBSE's case-based discussion assessments.

questions.q: Analyze how the interviewer Mukund Padmanabhan uses signallers to structure the Eco interview. Identify three specific signallers and explain the topic shift each signals.
questions.a: 1) "Which brings me to my next question" — shifts from Eco's academic style to his novelistic fame. 2) "Could the huge success of the novel have anything to do with the fact that it dealt with a period of medieval history that..." — shifts from sales figures to thematic analysis of The Name of the Rose. 3) "But let me tell you another story" — shifts from publisher expectations to the anecdote about the American publisher's 3,000-copy estimate. A wrong answer that lists linkers (e.g., "Over 40") as signallers shows the student cannot distinguish cohesive continuity from structural transitions — a distinction the NCERT "Noticing discourse linkers and signallers" section explicitly teaches and board exams test in discourse analysis questions.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The interview is a supremely serviceable medium of communication" (Denis Brian, Part I). Defend or challenge this using evidence from both parts of the chapter, considering the power dynamic Brian mentions.
questions.a: The statement holds but requires qualification. Defense: Brian's claim is validated by Eco's interview — millions learn about semiotics, medieval history, and creative process through this single conversation. Challenge: Part I shows the power dynamic cuts both ways — interviewers hold "unprecedented power" (Brian), but celebrities like Kipling and Carroll resist, reclaiming agency by refusal. Eco himself redirects the "novelist" label ("I consider myself a university professor who writes novels on Sundays"). Thus, the medium is serviceable only when power is negotiated, not assumed. A wrong answer that simply agrees without addressing the power asymmetry reveals the student accepts the text's surface claim without critical evaluation — exactly what CBSE competency questions penalize.

questions.q: Create a 3-minute interview role-play script between a student journalist and a peer portraying Umberto Eco, incorporating at least four discourse linkers and two signallers from the textbook, covering Eco's "interstices" concept and his view on The Name of the Rose's success.
questions.a: A successful script will: (1) Open with a signaller ("Let me start by asking..."), (2) Use linkers like "that," "which," "this" to connect Eco's responses to follow-ups, (3) Include "But let me tell you another story" before the publisher anecdote, (4) Use "Which brings me to" before the success question, (5) Have Eco say "I work in empty spaces... interstices" and "Nobody can predict it" verbatim or paraphrased. A poor script that reads like a monologue or lacks signallers shows the student views interviews as Q&A lists rather than co-constructed conversations — missing the chapter's core discourse lesson that interviews are collaborative meaning-making, not extraction.
